docs.title: Takeaway From the reports I found
Takeaway #1: Enumerate Versions, Not Just Ports. Don't just find open doors; find out exactly what kind of door it is. Use scan options like nmap -sV to aggressively probe for service versions.

Takeaway #2: Use searchsploit First, but Master Google Fu. Your local searchsploit is the quickest way to find public exploits. If that fails, use precise Google searches (e.g., "vsftpd 2.3.4" exploit PoC github") to find less-official, but potentially working, code.

Takeaway #3: Never Run Public Exploits Blindly. Always read the source code of an exploit before running it. Understand how it works, what it does to the target, and what you need to modify (like IP addresses and ports) for it to work correctly.

docs.title: Nmap Scanning 🗺️
docs.text: Nmap (Network Mapper) is an essential tool for network discovery and security auditing. It's used to discover hosts and services on a computer network by sending packets and analyzing the responses.

docs.title: Default Script & Version Scan
docs.text: nmap -sC -sV <target> -oA <output>

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text:
• -sC: Run default scripts for vulnerability detection
  • -sV: Detect service versions on open ports
  • <target>: IP address or hostname to scan (e.g., 10.10.10.5)
  • -oA: Save results in all formats (.nmap, .gnmap, .xml)

docs.title: Full Port Scan (All 65,535 Ports)
docs.text:
By default, Nmap only scans the top 1,000 most common ports. To be thorough, you should always perform a full port scan to check for services running on non-standard ports.

nmap -p- <target> -oA <output>

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text: • -p-: This is a shorthand that tells Nmap to scan all TCP ports from 1 to 65,535. It's much faster than typing -p 1-65535.

docs.title: Basic UDP Scan
docs.text:
While TCP scans are more common, it's important not to forget about UDP services like DNS, SNMP, or Kerberos.

sudo nmap -sU <target>

sudo nmap -sU --min-rate 10000  #for faster

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text: • -sU: This flag explicitly tells Nmap to perform a UDP scan.

docs.title: Nmap all ports filter into service scan
docs.text:
cat nmap/all_ports.nmap  | awk -F'/' '/open/ {print $1}' | paste -sd ','

sudo nmap -sC -sV -p "$(cat nmap/all_ports.nmap | awk -F'/' '/open/ {print $1}' | paste -sd ',')" 192.168.184.40

docs.title: MySQL Database Fuzzing & Testing 🗄️
docs.text: MySQL is one of the most popular open-source relational database management systems. During penetration testing, MySQL databases are often targeted for information gathering, privilege escalation, and data extraction.

docs.title: Interactive Connection Parameters
docs.text:
Enter MySQL connection details:

Host Username Database

docs.title: Interactive Connection
docs.text:
Connect to a MySQL database using the command line client:

mysql -u <username> -h <host> -p <database>

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text:
• -u: Username for the MySQL connection
  • -h: Host/IP address of the MySQL server
  • -p: Prompt for password (more secure than inline password)
  • database: Target database name (optional)

docs.title: One-liner SQL Execution
docs.text:
SQL Command:

Generate

Execute SQL commands directly from the command line without entering interactive mode:

mysql -u <username> -p<password> -h <host> <database> -e '<sql-command>;'

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text:
• -p<password>: Password directly in command (no space between -p and password)
  • -e: Execute the following SQL command and exit
  • '<sql-command>;': SQL command enclosed in quotes

docs.title: Dump Database
docs.text: mysqldump -u <username> -p<password> -h <host> <database> > db.sql

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text:
• -p<password>: Password directly in command (no space between -p and password)
  • -e: Execute the following SQL command and exit
  • '<sql-command>;': SQL command enclosed in quotes

docs.title: Common MySQL Fuzzing Techniques
docs.text:
View running processes:

mysql -u <username> -p<password> -h <host> -e 'SHOW PROCESSLIST;'

docs.title: Tips for MySQL Fuzzing
docs.text:
1. Always test with minimal privileges first - Start with limited user accounts
  2. Use information_schema - Rich source of metadata about database structure
  3. Check for default credentials - root/root, admin/admin, etc.
  4. Test different ports - MySQL default is 3306, but check other ports
  5. Look for configuration files - my.cnf often contains sensitive information
  6. Check for UDF (User Defined Functions) - Can lead to code execution

docs.title: Web Fuzzing Using FFUF 🔍
docs.text: FFUF (Fuzz Faster U Fool) is a fast web fuzzer written in Go. It's designed for discovering elements and content within web applications by fuzzing parameters, directories, virtual hosts, and more.

docs.title: Installation and Setup
docs.text: For FFUF installation instructions, please visit the official documentation: https://github.com/ffuf/ffuf#installation

docs.title: Clone SecLists Repository
docs.text:
SecLists provides comprehensive wordlists for security testing. Clone it to /opt directory for easy access:

sudo git clone https://github.com/danielmiessler/SecLists.git /opt/SecLists

docs.title: Interactive Domain Input
docs.text:
Enter your target domain to complete commands:

Generate

docs.title: Virtual Host (VHost) Fuzzing
docs.text:
Virtual host fuzzing is used to discover subdomains or virtual hosts on a web server. This technique is particularly useful during reconnaissance to find hidden or forgotten virtual hosts.

ffuf -w /opt/SecLists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -u http://<yourdomain.com>/ -H "Host: FUZZ.<yourdomain.com>"

docs.title: Parameter Breakdown
docs.text:
• -w: Wordlist file path (using SecLists subdomain wordlist)
  • -u: Target URL (IP address of the target)
  • -H: Custom HTTP header (Host header with FUZZ placeholder)
  • -mc: Match HTTP status codes (successful responses)

docs.title: Content Discovery Fuzzing
docs.text:
Content discovery involves finding hidden files, directories, and endpoints on web applications. This helps identify backup files, configuration files, admin panels, and other potentially sensitive resources.

common.txt (Small - 4,713 entries) raft-medium-directory.txt (Large - 220,560 entries) 
ffuf -w <wordlist-path> -u http://<yourdomain.com>/FUZZ

docs.title: Numeric ID Fuzzing
docs.text: ffuf -u http://<yourdomain.com>/?id=FUZZ -w <(seq 1 10000)

docs.title: Useful Flags
docs.text:
• -c: Colorize output
  • -v: Verbose output
  • -t: Number of concurrent threads (default: 40)
  • -mc: Match specific HTTP status codes
  • -fc: Filter out specific HTTP status codes
  • -fs: Filter out responses by size
  • -fl: Filter out responses by line count

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
1. Always start with smaller wordlists and gradually move to larger ones
  2. Use -c flag for colored output to easily spot successful findings
  3. Combine with -fs to filter out common response sizes (often 404 pages)
  4. Use -t to adjust thread count based on your connection and target capacity
  5. Save results with -o output.json for later analysis
